Vera opens a book as thick as a door. She writes your name, your pathway, your sequence. Under "cause" she writes, without asking: burned.

Then she leafs back without meaning to, and you see it too: twelve entries from this year are struck out. All with the same ink, all with the same straight stroke. No cross, no line upward. Simply gone.

"That wasn't me," Vera says quietly. "At night the book lies in the Crown Archive. Ask Hesk. He carries those who fall. He knows where they go."

But ash flies. In Calderwick it flies into the pits: into the Old Typesetting Works, into the Sorting Pit, into the Null Foundation."

Ruth lays the three pages under glass and does not breathe. After an hour she reads aloud:

"Lucius Starling. Fell forty-one years ago. Pathway: illegible. Sequence 4. Cause: burned." Beneath it, in another hand: "Departed on the second train. Guarantor: O. Wetherby." And beneath that, twelve names, all struck out with the same straight stroke.

Ruth puts down the magnifier. "He was one of us. He harvested twelve of the fallen to grow heavy enough for the journey. And Wetherby vouched for him." She looks at you. "The Crown Archive is still harvesting. For him."

You think of Kettlegate. Of nine cases Starling called "the harvest". He did not begin there. He finished there, down here.

Above the Crown Archive a track ends in mid-air. A faceless conductor waits beside it, for years, people say.

"The train upward is running again," he says. "Not for you. Not as you are now. Whoever wants to last up there comes as a saint, and even saints burn there without a guarantor."

He nods towards a second track that leads downward, behind the Archive Hall. "The way up sometimes begins down below."

Behind the Archive Hall stands a freight train loaded with empty crates. Wetherby's waybill fits every single one: BRIARHOLT, CURE.

You do not climb into a crate. You sit on one. The train starts to roll, not upward but down, through fog and frost, until the air smells of herbal brew.

Calderwick stays behind you. Ida and Noel do not wave, they are cooking. Somewhere ahead lies a spa town where the fallen are "healed", and at the end of the line, at the very top, Starling waits for what is cooked there.

Zwischen geschmolzenen Lettern klemmt ei: A charred sheet is wedged between molten type. The lines are those of the Book of the Fallen, the writing is ash. Ruth might be able to read it.

You lever the lid open. Inside, a woman lies curled up on straw, hands around her knees. Where wings should be, two scars glow. She blinks into the light of the pit.

"Ida," she says before you ask. "Ida Bellcross. Tell Noel I am hungry."

The lid bears a stamp: CROWN ARCHIVE, FILED. Below it, in chalk: BRIARHOLT, CURE.
Unter einem Haufen leerer Rohrpostkapsel: Under a heap of empty pneumatic capsules lies a singed page. A stamp is still visible at the edge: Crown Archive, filed.

Hinter der Verteilanlage läuft ein Rohr:
Behind the distribution plant a pipe does not run into the greenhouses but straight up, through the roof, into the fog. It is warm as a body. A brass plate reads: CALDERWICK, CROWN ARCHIVE, ABOVE.

So this is the cure. What Greavesend takes from the patients is neither fever nor grief. It is their weight. It is boiled, bottled and sent up the line, past Calderwick, all the way to Starling. He needs it to stay up there.

You turn the valve shut. The pipe goes cold, from the bottom up, so slowly you can watch it. Somewhere above Calderwick, above the clouds, a man now sits on the steps of a throne and freezes.

He will not come down again. If you want him, you have to go up. As a saint you would still burn there. As an angel perhaps not.
